pages.title: INTRODUCTION
pages.html:
INTRODUCTION

The Leader in the Room

Leadership is a scored conversation with no pause.

Every other professional world in this series has a defined conversation window — the loan officer's call, the cold caller's thirty seconds, the BDM's lunch. Leadership does not have a window. Leadership is a continuous scored environment. The leader who walks into a room changes the score of every person in it before they have said a word. Their presence alone carries a Profit position built or eroded over months of prior interactions. Their tone in the first exchange sets the Love ceiling for the rest of the meeting. Their consistency — between what they say and what they do, between how they treat someone when things are going well and how they treat them when things are not — is the only currency that produces genuine trust, and it is being spent or saved in every conversation they have ever had with every person on their team.

Compliance is easy. If you hold authority over someone — their performance review, their compensation, their professional reputation — they will comply with your direction. They will deliver what is asked, meet the minimum standard, and keep their most honest assessments of your leadership to themselves. Compliance is the score produced by authority alone. It looks like leadership. It is not leadership.

Trust is different. Trust is the score produced by a leader who has demonstrated, repeatedly, in the specific texture of their conversations, that they are genuinely working for the person they are leading — not just directing them, not just developing them in the abstract, but actually in the room for them, running the moves that the conversation requires rather than the moves that protect the leader's position. Trust is not given because of title. It is built in the exchange after the performance review where the leader stayed in the room when they could have left. In the team meeting where the leader named the problem before someone else had to name it. In the one-on-one where the leader asked the question they were not sure they wanted the answer to.

This book scores those conversations. All of them. The full arc of the leadership relationship — from the first one-on-one with a new direct report to the most difficult conversation a leader will ever have in a professional setting. Nine characters. Eight conversations scored in depth, by movement, across the full arc of each exchange. Ten drills. A complete field guide for every leadership situation from a team that is performing to a team that is not.

◆

This book also introduces something that no other career Scorer edition has carried: the internal score running beneath the external one. Leadership is the professional world where the leader's internal conversation is most visible to the people they lead. The leader who has not done their own internal work before a difficult conversation is visible. The team can feel the difference between a leader who has cleared their own score before entering the room and one who is managing their own anxiety while trying to lead. That difference is in this book.

Profit. Love. Tax. Three scores running simultaneously in every leadership conversation. The leader who can read all three — in real time, across every character in their world — does not manage their team. They develop it. And development, built from hundreds of correctly scored conversations over months and years, is the only thing that produces the team every leader says they want and most leaders never have.

pages.title: PART ONE
pages.html:
PART ONE

The Leadership World

What leadership conversations actually are. Why most leaders produce compliance and call it trust.

pages.title: CHAPTER 1
pages.html:
CHAPTER 1

The Authority Trap

The authority trap is the most common and most invisible failure mode in leadership.

It works like this: a leader gives direction. The team complies. The leader observes compliance and concludes that the direction was good and that the team is aligned. The team, for its part, has delivered compliance without alignment — has executed the direction while withholding the assessment, the concern, the alternative perspective, the information the leader actually needed in order to give good direction in the first place. The leader never knows. The team always knows.

The authority trap is not about bad intentions. Most leaders who are caught in it are trying to lead well. They give thoughtful direction. They explain their reasoning. They make themselves available for questions. But they have, usually without knowing it, created a conversational environment in which honest feedback flows in one direction — downward — while the team's real assessments flow nowhere. The leader who asks "does anyone have concerns?" in a room where expressing concerns has historically cost people something will receive silence. The leader reads the silence as alignment. The silence is not alignment. It is the team having learned the correct answer to that question.

◆

The PLT framework diagnoses the authority trap precisely. Profit in a leadership conversation measures whether the team member believes the leader is in the room as a genuine thinking partner or as a direction-giver who has already decided. When Profit collapses — when the team member senses that the question is rhetorical — they exit the real conversation and enter the compliance performance.

Love in a leadership conversation measures something specific: does the team member feel that the leader sees them as an individual — their specific strengths, their specific development edges, their specific situation — or do they feel like a function being managed? The leader who knows their team members as people, who asks questions that could only be asked of this specific person rather than anyone with their job title, is building Love in a way that the leader who runs transactional one-on-ones never will.

Tax in a leadership conversation accumulates in the gap between what is said and what is meant. The leader who says "I trust your judgment" and then overrides the judgment creates Tax that does not disappear when the next task begins. The Tax of the gap between stated culture and experienced culture is the heaviest Tax in leadership — and it is invisible to the leader who is creating it.

pages.title: CHAPTER 2
pages.html:
CHAPTER 2

Why Good Leaders Lose Good People

The good people leave for the same reason the pipelines go cold in BDM work. The scores drained in conversations that appeared to be going fine.

The performance review that was technically accurate and completely impersonal. The one-on-one that stayed on task and never went below the surface. The team meeting where the leader solved the problem quickly and efficiently and the person who had a better solution quietly noted that the solution space was not actually open. None of these conversations were crises. None produced a visible score collapse. All of them produced a small, steady drain in Profit and Love that accumulated over eighteen months until the good person had a conversation with themselves one evening — the internal scored monologue — and concluded that the growth they were looking for was not available here.

The leader almost always says the same thing when they leave: "I had no idea they were unhappy." This is usually honest. The leader was not reading the score. They were tracking outputs — deliverables, deadlines, performance metrics — while the relationship score that determines whether the person is engaged or simply performing was draining beneath the surface of every meeting they attended.

◆

The scorer reads the score beneath the output. They notice the team member who gives shorter answers in one-on-ones than they did six months ago. They catch the shift from the person who used to raise concerns to the person who now says "sounds good." They feel the difference in a team meeting between a room that is engaged and a room that is present — the same people, different scores, visible to anyone who is watching the right things.

pages.title: PART TWO
pages.html:
PART TWO

The Nine Characters

Everyone in the leadership world. The complete cast of the conversations that build or end careers.

01

The Direct Report

The Direct Report is the leader's most important scored relationship and the one where the scoring errors are most consequential.

The Direct Report has three primary needs in their relationship with their leader, and the degree to which those needs are met determines whether they are engaged or merely compliant. They need to be seen — to experience the specific, individualized attention that tells them they are known as a person rather than managed as a function. They need to be heard — to have the genuine experience, not just the performative invitation, of their assessments and concerns entering the leader's thinking. And they need to be developed — to feel the leader actively working on their growth rather than simply measuring their current output.

Most leaders meet one of these needs reasonably well. The leader who is good at recognition meets the seen need but often neglects the heard need. The leader who is good at feedback meets the developed need but can neglect the seen need — the feedback is precise but the person feels like a project rather than a human. The leader who is good at inclusion meets the heard need but can neglect the developed need — everyone is invited into the conversation but the hard developmental feedback that would actually grow the person is avoided.

◆

Reading the Direct Report's score: Profit — do they bring you their real problems or only the ones they have already solved? The direct report who only surfaces resolved issues has learned that bringing you an open problem is more costly than solving it alone. Love — do they share context you did not ask for? Genuine Love in a reporting relationship produces voluntary disclosure. Tax — how often do they use the phrase "just wanted to make sure we're aligned"? Alignment-checking is Tax made audible. It signals the person is managing your reaction rather than sharing their actual thinking.

02

The High Performer

The High Performer is the most consistently mismanaged relationship in leadership.

The error is always the same: the leader stops developing the High Performer because the High Performer does not appear to need development. Output is excellent. Deliverables arrive early. The High Performer requires less maintenance than the rest of the team, so the leader allocates their attention to the people who are demanding it. The High Performer notices this. Not immediately. Over time. They notice that the one-on-ones have become status checks. They notice that the leader's hardest problems go to someone else. They notice that the conversation about their career — their actual aspirations, the work that would challenge them at the edge of their capability — has not happened in recent memory.

The High Performer does not complain about this. They continue performing. And then one day they accept a role somewhere else that offers what the leader stopped providing: the genuine developmental attention that makes work feel like more than excellent delivery.

◆

The leader who retains High Performers does one thing differently: they treat the High Performer's development as a higher priority than the High Performer's output. They are willing to put the High Performer in situations where they will struggle — where their current capability is genuinely insufficient and the growth required is real — because they understand that the High Performer who is not growing is already leaving, even if they have not said so and do not know it yet.

Reading the High Performer's score: Profit — are they still bringing you their most ambitious thinking, or have their contributions become reliable and safe? Love — when did you last have a conversation about their career that was not tied to a performance cycle? Tax — have they stopped asking for feedback? The high performer who stops asking has stopped expecting anything useful from the asking.

03

The Underperformer

The Underperformer is the conversation most leaders avoid longest and handle worst.

By the time most leaders have the formal performance conversation, three things have already happened that make it harder. The underperformance has been visible to the rest of the team for long enough that they have begun adjusting around it — covering, compensating, quietly resenting the accommodation. The underperformer themselves has either convinced themselves the performance is acceptable or has developed a private narrative about why the expectations are unreasonable. And the leader has built enough Tax from the delay that the conversation arrives freighted with months of unexpressed concern that makes it feel like a verdict rather than a coaching exchange.

◆

The scorer addresses underperformance early. Not punitively — early. The earliest performance conversation is the one that still has the most Love in it, the most Profit available for a genuine development exchange, and the least Tax from accumulated delay. The leader who runs Move 02 — the Honest Strike — at the first sign of a performance concern, specifically and without judgment, is the leader who gives the underperformer the best chance of developing before the situation has become a verdict.

04

The Peer Leader

The Peer Leader is the leader's most complex scored relationship because it has no formal authority structure and therefore no fallback position.

In a peer leadership relationship, Profit is entirely earned. There is no title that produces it automatically. The peer who brings something to the cross-functional meeting that changes the quality of the decision has built Profit. The peer leader relationship also runs the highest-visibility Tax in leadership. When a leader treats a peer relationship as a competitive arena — where the goal is to protect their team's interests rather than to genuinely collaborate — that Tax is visible to everyone in the room, including the executives above them.

The scorer in a peer leadership environment runs Move 07 — Family Inclusion — in its professional form. The peer who proactively brings other teams into the thinking before the decision is made, who designs solutions that account for the adjacent team's constraints without being asked to, is running the highest-Profit move available in a peer relationship.

05

The Executive Above

The Executive Above is the leader's most carefully managed relationship and the one most in need of honest scoring.

The Profit collapse in the Executive relationship almost always comes from one of two sources. The first: the Executive discovers a problem that the leader knew about and did not surface. The second: the Executive loses confidence in the leader's judgment because the leader never brings them genuine assessments, only managed ones. The highest-Profit move in an Executive relationship is the one most leaders never run: surfacing a problem before the Executive has to ask about it.

06

The Team

The Team is the audience for the leader's most public scored performance and the relationship where inconsistency is most expensive.

A team scores its leader across dozens of data points simultaneously: how they run meetings, how they handle disagreement, how they behave under pressure, how they treat the lowest-status person in the room, how consistent their stated values are with their observable behavior. The team compiles this scoring continuously and compares notes informally. By the time a leader has been in place for ninety days, the team has a fairly precise collective read on who this leader actually is — not who they say they are, but who they are when the situation is difficult and the stakes are real.

Team Love builds in moments the leader often does not identify as significant. The meeting where the leader took the blame for a team failure rather than distributing it. The public acknowledgment that was specific rather than generic. The moment of visible uncertainty where the leader said "I don't know" and the team saw that not-knowing was something the leader could hold without panic.

07

The Skeptic

Every team has a Skeptic. The person whose facial expression in the meeting communicates assessment rather than agreement. The person who asks the question everyone else was not going to ask.

Most leaders handle the Skeptic incorrectly in one of two ways. They dismiss the skepticism — treating it as resistance rather than intelligence — and in doing so lose the most accurate feedback instrument on their team. Or they manage the Skeptic privately, neutralizing their skepticism before it reaches the group, and in doing so signal to everyone else that authentic assessment is something to be managed rather than welcomed.

pages.title: PART TWO (cont. 2)
pages.html:
The scorer treats the Skeptic as the team's highest-Profit voice. The Skeptic who asks the difficult question in a meeting and receives a genuine response — not a defense, a genuine engagement with the concern — teaches the whole team something about the kind of thinking that is welcome in this leader's room. The Skeptic who is received well becomes one of the most powerful advocates for the leader's direction. Not because they agreed immediately. Because they were engaged honestly and found the engagement worth trusting.

08

The Exiting Employee

The Exiting Employee is the most honest relationship a leader will ever have with a member of their team — and the one they almost always handle worst.

When someone gives notice, most leaders conduct the exit conversation as a procedural formality. And in doing so they miss the single most honest feedback opportunity available in the leadership relationship. The person who is leaving has nothing to protect. Their assessment of the leader, the team, and the organization is the most unfiltered data available. The leader who runs the exit conversation as a genuine scored exchange — who asks not "what brings you to this decision" but "what would have needed to be true here for you to stay?" — is running Move 04 in its most complete leadership form.

09

The New Leader

The New Leader — either the leader themselves in a new role or someone they are bringing in below them — is the character who runs the highest-Tax entry in the leadership world.

Every new leader enters with a deficit of trust that must be built from the first conversation. The new leader who runs the first ninety days as a listening and scoring exercise — who builds Profit through demonstrated understanding of what already exists before proposing what should be different — is the new leader who inherits a functional team rather than spending the first year rebuilding trust that was damaged by arriving with answers before the questions were fully heard.

pages.title: PART THREE
pages.html:
PART THREE

The Leader's Score

The leadership score is always running. The leader who does not know this is the leader everyone else is scoring.

The Visible Internal Score

The leadership world is the only professional environment in the Scorer Series where the leader's internal score is directly visible to the people around them.

In cold calling, the prospect cannot see whether the caller has anxiety about the call. In BDM work, the contact cannot see whether the BDM is genuinely invested. In loan officer work, the buyer cannot see whether the LO is managing their own discomfort when delivering a condition. In leadership, the team can see all of it.

A team reads their leader's internal score through dozens of observable signals: the leader's body language in the meeting where the bad news arrived, the specific quality of their listening in the one-on-one, the tone they take with the lowest-performing team member versus the highest-performing one, how long they take to make eye contact with the person who gave them the unwelcome feedback.

◆

The leadership application of the Internal Scorer doctrine: before every difficult conversation, the leader needs to know their own score. Are they entering the performance conversation with a Profit of genuine development intent or a Profit built from months of frustration they have not processed? Are they entering the one-on-one with a Love that is real and present or a Love that is going through its scheduled motions? Is there Tax they are carrying from a prior interaction with this person that has not been cleared? If any of these answers is honest and unflattering, the leader needs to do their internal work before they enter the room. The team will know whether they did.

The Leadership Signature Move

Of all nine moves in the Scorer doctrine, one is the foundation of everything a leader builds.

Move 02 — the Honest Strike.

Not because leaders are more dishonest than other professionals. Because the structural incentives of leadership create more pressure toward managed truth than any other professional environment. The leader who is honest about uncertainty loses the appearance of certainty that authority is supposed to produce. The leader who is honest about a team failure loses the appearance of control that stakeholders expect. The leader who is honest with an underperformer creates a difficult conversation they could have avoided.

Every one of these incentives points toward managed truth. And every one of them, when followed, produces the exact cost it was designed to avoid — only later, with compound interest.

◆

The Honest Strike in leadership is not about being blunt. It is about being early and specific. Early: the first time the concern is clear, not the fourth time it has become unavoidable. Specific: this behavior, this impact, this conversation — not "there are some concerns about performance" but "in the last two presentations you have not accounted for the cost implications and that has created problems in three downstream decisions."

The leader who runs the Honest Strike early and specifically is the leader who gives people something they can act on. The leader who waits until early has become unavoidable and specific has become a list has not been developing their team. They have been avoiding their team while calling it patience.

pages.title: PART FOUR
pages.html:
PART FOUR

The Conversations

The leadership world scored across every relationship. Every conversation by movement. Every score earned.

The One-on-One

The conversation that determines whether the relationship is real or managed

The one-on-one is the most important recurring conversation in a leader's calendar and the one most consistently run as a status check rather than a developmental exchange.

Marcus is a senior manager. Alicia is one of his most capable direct reports. They have been having weekly one-on-ones for eight months. The meetings run on time. They cover what is current. Marcus considers the relationship strong. Alicia has been wondering for three months whether to take a call she received from a recruiter.

◆

pages.title: MOVEMENT ONE THE STATUS CHECK
pages.html:
MOVEMENT ONE THE STATUS CHECK

Marcus: "How is the Meridian project tracking?"

Alicia: "On schedule. We hit the milestone yesterday. Team's in good shape."

Marcus: "Good. The finance review — any blockers?"

Alicia: "Nothing I can't handle. I'll have it by Thursday."

Marcus makes a note. This is their fourth exchange and they have been in the meeting for six minutes. This is the pattern.

Marcus: "How are you feeling about Q4 workload overall?"

Alicia: "It's manageable."

"Manageable" is a closed answer. Marcus does not open it.

Marcus: "Good. Anything else you need from me?"

A pause. Alicia has three things she could say. She says the easiest one.

Alicia: "I'm good for now."

The meeting ends in eleven minutes.

THE SCORE

The Status Check — The Real Conversation Is Not Happening

PROFIT 54 ▼ 10|LOVE 52 ▼ 12|TAX 48 ▲ 12

MOVE MISSED DIAGNOSTIC — MOVE 03 NOT RUNNING

Marcus ran logistical questions and received logistical answers. The score on both sides of this relationship has been drifting for months because the one-on-one has never moved below the status layer. Profit is declining because Alicia no longer expects the meeting to produce anything more than task coverage. Love is declining because eight months of eleven-minute meetings that end with "anything else you need from me?" have communicated, without Marcus intending it, that the meeting's purpose is completion rather than connection. Tax is building because Alicia's three unsaid things — including her evaluation of the recruiter's call — are accumulating as internal cost with no legitimate outlet. The question "how are you feeling about Q4 workload" was the opening. "Manageable" was the door closing. Marcus did not knock.

pages.title: MOVEMENT TWO THE QUESTION THAT CHANGES THE MEETING
pages.html:
MOVEMENT TWO THE QUESTION THAT CHANGES THE MEETING

Four weeks later. Same meeting. Marcus came with a different question.

Marcus: "Before we go through the usual — I want to ask you something different. What's the work that would genuinely stretch you right now? Not what's on your plate. What's not on your plate that should be?"

Alicia looks at him. This is not the meeting she prepared for.

Alicia: "That's... a different kind of question."

Marcus: "I know. I think we've been running these meetings as status checks and I want to change that. So — what is it? What are you not doing that you think you should be?"

A longer pause. Alicia is deciding how honest to be.

Alicia: "The vendor strategy work. I've had a perspective on it for six months but it's always been handled above my level. I think the current approach has a structural problem that isn't going to be visible until Q2 and by then it will be expensive to correct."

Marcus: "Tell me."

THE SCORE

The Question That Changes the Meeting — Genuine Diagnostic

PROFIT 72 ▲ 18|LOVE 76 ▲ 24|TAX 24 ▼ 24

MOVE DIAGNOSTIC OPENING + INTELLIGENCE TRANSFER — MOVES 03

Marcus ran the diagnostic question — "what's not on your plate that should be" — in its purest leadership form. Love builds 24 points — the largest single Love movement in this conversation — because Alicia has finally experienced a leader who came to the one-on-one wanting something from her that was not deliverable status. She disclosed the vendor strategy concern, which she had been carrying for six months. That disclosure was the test. Marcus's response — "tell me," two words, complete attention — is the move that determines whether the test results in genuine development or in Alicia recalibrating back to managed status. He passed the test.

pages.title: MOVEMENT THREE THE FULL DISCLOSURE
pages.html:
MOVEMENT THREE THE FULL DISCLOSURE

Alicia: "The current vendor consolidation assumes consistent volume across all three regions. Our Southeast data has been inconsistent for two quarters. If volume drops in that region by fifteen percent — which based on the trend it will — the consolidation economics break. The savings don't materialize and we've already restructured the contracts. The people running the strategy haven't seen the Southeast trend because it's buried in operational reports that nobody reads at that level."

Marcus is listening. Not managing — listening. He does not reach for his phone. He does not fill the silence between Alicia's sentences.

Marcus: "How confident are you in this read?"

Alicia: "Eighty percent. There's a scenario where the Southeast stabilizes that I can't fully rule out. But I'd want someone to pressure-test the assumption before the contracts go final."

Marcus: "Who else knows you've been looking at this?"

Alicia: "No one. I didn't know where to bring it."

Marcus sets his pen down.

Marcus: "You should have been able to bring it here. That's on me. I want you to write this up — not formally, just your analysis — and I want to present it with you in the Q3 review. You'll have the room."

THE SCORE

The Full Disclosure — Six Months of Intelligence Enters the Conversation

PROFIT 88 ▲ 16|LOVE 92 ▲ 16|TAX 10 ▼ 14

MOVE OWNERSHIP MOVE + PATH FORWARD — MOVES 05 & 09

Marcus ran Move 05 — "that's on me" — immediately and specifically. He did not explain why the prior meetings had been what they were. He owned the gap and moved directly to the path forward. Love reaches its highest point because Alicia heard a leader take accountability for a structural failure in their relationship and offer a specific opportunity as its correction. "You'll have the room" is the most important sentence — it is the leader converting the discovered intelligence into an opportunity for the person who held it. Profit is dominant because both people are now working with accurate information about both the vendor strategy and the relationship. The recruiter's call, for Alicia, has become slightly less interesting.

◆

The Performance Conversation

The most avoided conversation in leadership. The most necessary one.

The performance conversation that is run correctly is not a verdict. It is a development exchange with a very specific piece of intelligence at its center: the gap between current performance and required performance, named precisely, without the softening that makes the gap invisible.

Sandra is a director. Devon has been on her team for fourteen months. His work is technically proficient and chronically late. Sandra has mentioned the timeline issue twice in passing. This is the conversation where she names it directly.

◆

pages.title: MOVEMENT ONE THE HONEST OPENING
pages.html:
MOVEMENT ONE THE HONEST OPENING

Sandra: "I want to talk about something directly today — the timeline pattern on your deliverables. I want to tell you specifically what I've observed and then I want to hear from you."

Devon's expression shifts slightly. He was not expecting this to be what the meeting was about.

Devon: "Okay."

Sandra: "In the last six months, eight of your twelve deliverables have come in after the agreed deadline. The average delay is three days. I've noted this twice in our one-on-ones but I haven't given you a direct conversation about it, and I should have done that sooner. The pattern is affecting downstream work — three times this quarter, other team members have had to adjust their timelines. That's the specific situation. What's your read on it?"

A pause. Devon is processing whether this is safe to be honest in.

Devon: "I've known it's been an issue. I've been trying to manage it on my own."

Sandra: "Tell me more about that."

THE SCORE

The Honest Opening — The Gap Named Precisely

PROFIT 72 ▲ 8|LOVE 68 ▲ 6|TAX 32 ▲ 6

MOVE HONEST STRIKE — MOVE 02

Sandra ran Move 02 with the specific elements that make performance conversations developmentally useful: she named the pattern (eight of twelve), the magnitude (three-day average delay), the downstream impact (three timeline adjustments), and her own accountability (she should have had this conversation sooner). The self-accountability is critical — it separates this from the performance conversation that feels like prosecution. Profit builds because Devon now has accurate information about the actual scope of the issue. Love builds slightly because Sandra's acknowledgment that she should have been clearer sooner signals that this is a development conversation, not a verdict. The question "what's your read on it?" gives Devon the floor. His answer determines the second movement.

pages.title: MOVEMENT TWO THE REAL CAUSE
pages.html:
MOVEMENT TWO THE REAL CAUSE

Devon: "The technical work takes longer than I estimate. I'm accurate on the analysis component but the documentation and stakeholder prep consistently take twice what I budget for them. I've been trying to absorb the overrun by working longer instead of adjusting the deadline earlier or flagging it."

Sandra: "Why not flag it?"

Devon: "Honestly? I didn't want to be the person who couldn't manage their workload. I've seen other people flag overruns and it changed how they were perceived."

Sandra is quiet for a moment. That is useful information about the team culture she has been running.

Sandra: "What you're describing — trying to absorb the problem rather than surface it — that's a culture problem, not a performance problem. You should be able to flag a timeline risk without it costing you. That's on me to make true, not just say. What I need from you in the near term is different: flag early. Not when you've missed the deadline. When you see it coming, which you clearly can."

THE SCORE

The Real Cause — The Culture Gap Surfaces

PROFIT 82 ▲ 10|LOVE 84 ▲ 16|TAX 18 ▼ 14

MOVE FRAME RESET + OWNERSHIP MOVE — MOVES 01 & 05

Sandra ran Move 01 — Frame Reset: she reframed Devon's behavior from a performance failure to a cultural signal, which is accurate. Devon was not failing to manage timelines — he was managing them privately because surfacing problems had been costly. That reframe is not an excuse for Devon — the late deliverables still happened. But it correctly identifies where the intervention is needed. Then Sandra ran Move 05 immediately: "that's on me to make true, not just say." She took accountability for the culture that produced the behavior she has been managing as a performance issue. Love builds 16 points because Devon just saw a leader receive his disclosure and respond by expanding her own accountability rather than contracting it.

pages.title: MOVEMENT THREE THE AGREEMENT
pages.html:
MOVEMENT THREE THE AGREEMENT

Devon: "I can do that. Flag early instead of absorb."

Sandra: "Here is what I'll do in return — when you flag, I want to have a specific agreement about what the response looks like. Not just 'let me know' — I'll give you a defined path for timeline risk. And I want to check in on this specifically in three weeks — not the deliverables, the flagging behavior. Does that work?"

Devon: "Yes."

The meeting takes twenty-eight minutes. Devon leaves with a specific behavior to change and a specific environment change he was just promised. Sandra leaves with an observation about her team culture she did not have before she walked in.

THE SCORE

The Agreement — Both Parties Have Something Specific to Do

PROFIT 88 ▲ 6|LOVE 88 ▲ 4|TAX 12 ▼ 6

MOVE PATH FORWARD — MOVE 09

Sandra ran Move 09 with two elements that are both necessary: Devon's specific behavior change and her own specific structural change. The performance conversation that ends with only the direct report having a commitment is not a development conversation — it is a managed verdict with a polite wrapper. The conversation that ends with both parties having a specific commitment is a development exchange. The three-week check-in is the Path Forward's most important element: it creates accountability for both commitments and signals that Sandra is managing the relationship, not just the deliverable.

◆

The Vision Conversation

When the leader needs the team to go somewhere they cannot fully see yet

The vision conversation is the highest-stakes team conversation a leader runs — and the one where the gap between a leader who has scored their internal state and one who has not is most visible.

Jordan leads a team of eleven people. The organization is restructuring. Roles are changing, priorities are shifting, and two team members are moving to different parts of the organization. Jordan has been told the direction. He believes in it. He also knows his team has not been fully told, and that what he is about to say will require them to change work they have been executing well.

◆

pages.title: MOVEMENT ONE THE HONEST FRAME
pages.html:
MOVEMENT ONE THE HONEST FRAME

Jordan: "I want to start with what I know is true and what I don't know yet. What I know: we are restructuring the team around two focus areas instead of four, effective January. What that means for each of you specifically — your roles, your current projects, how the transition will be managed — I'm still working through with leadership and I will have specifics by the end of next week. What I don't know yet: I can't tell you today how every role maps to the new structure. I want to be honest about that rather than give you a polished answer I'm not sure about."

The room is quiet. The team is processing.

Keisha: "Are there layoffs involved?"

The direct question. Jordan was expecting it.

Jordan: "I don't have full information on that yet. What I can tell you is that the goal of the restructure is to focus the team's work, not to reduce its size. But I won't tell you that means no changes to headcount because I don't know that with certainty and I'm not going to tell you something I'm not sure of."

THE SCORE

The Honest Frame — Uncertainty Named, Not Managed

PROFIT 80 ▲ 12|LOVE 78 ▲ 10|TAX 22 ▼ 6

MOVE HONEST STRIKE — MOVE 02 WITH TEAM

Jordan ran Move 02 with the team in the most difficult leadership context: delivering incomplete information about a change that affects every person in the room. The moves that make this land correctly: he named what he knows and what he does not know as separate categories without blurring them. He said "I won't tell you something I'm not sure of" — not as a hedge but as a commitment. Profit builds because the team can now calibrate their understanding accurately rather than trying to read between lines that have been managed to a polish. Love builds because the team sees a leader who is willing to hold uncertainty visibly rather than performing confidence he does not have. The team does not have the answer they wanted. They have the honest answer, which is better than the managed one.

pages.title: MOVEMENT TWO THE SKEPTIC SPEAKS
pages.html:
MOVEMENT TWO THE SKEPTIC SPEAKS

Tyler: "Why restructure toward two focus areas instead of staying with four? We've been executing on all four. What's the argument?"

Tyler is the team's Skeptic. He asks the question with a tone that is not hostile but is not easily satisfied. The room waits to see how Jordan handles it.

Jordan: "It's a fair question. The argument is resource density — that we can go deeper and build more durable capability in two areas than we can produce competent output across four. The counterargument is exactly what you're saying: we've been executing on four and the work has been good. My honest read is that the counterargument has merit and I made it to leadership. The decision came back as a direction, not an invitation to continue the debate. So I'm executing it. I think there is real upside in the two-focus model if we do it well. I also think there is transition cost that will be real before the upside materializes."

A longer pause. Tyler is processing the answer.

Tyler: "I appreciate that you said you made the counterargument."

Jordan: "I wanted you to know that it was heard up the chain. It didn't change the direction. But it was heard."

THE SCORE

The Skeptic Speaks — Honest Engagement With the Hard Question

PROFIT 88 ▲ 8|LOVE 86 ▲ 8|TAX 14 ▼ 8

MOVE HONEST STRIKE + EVIDENCE MIRROR — MOVES 02 & 04

Jordan ran two moves simultaneously in response to Tyler's challenge. The Honest Strike: he acknowledged the counterargument's merit, disclosed that he made it, and disclosed that it did not change the decision. This is one of the hardest sequences in leadership communication — being honest with the team about a direction you had reservations about. The Evidence Mirror: "I wanted you to know it was heard up the chain." Jordan is giving Tyler and the team the information they need to understand the full picture — not just the decision, but the process. The team can now see: the decision was not made without their concerns in view. It was made after those concerns were raised and considered. That distinction is the difference between the team that accepts a direction they disagree with and the team that resists one.

pages.title: MOVEMENT THREE THE COMMITMENT
pages.html:
MOVEMENT THREE THE COMMITMENT

Jordan: "Here is what I can commit to for the next three weeks. By Friday I'll have the specific role mapping for each of you — individual conversations, not a group announcement. By the end of next week I'll have the project transition plan so you know what happens to current work. And I'll hold space in every one-on-one for questions about this specifically. What I need from this team is your real concerns, surfaced to me rather than to each other in the hallway. I can't address what I don't know about."

The room's energy is different now. Not relieved — this is not a relieving situation. But present. The team is with Jordan rather than behind a protective layer of managed response.

Keisha: "The individual conversations by Friday — that's real?"

Jordan: "That's real. I'll start tomorrow."

THE SCORE

The Commitment — Specific, Accountable, Human

PROFIT 90 ▲ 2|LOVE 90 ▲ 4|TAX 10 ▼ 4

MOVE PATH FORWARD — MOVE 09

Jordan ran Move 09 with three specific commitments — role mapping, transition plan, one-on-one space — each with specific timelines. The move that elevates this Path Forward: "I can't address what I don't know about." Jordan has explicitly named that the team's real concerns need to surface to him rather than circulating informally. He has made a specific ask of the team in exchange for his specific commitments. The score at the end of this conversation is high not because the situation is good — it is a genuine organizational disruption — but because the leader and the team are in the same honest room about it.

◆

The High Performer

The conversation most leaders are too comfortable to have

The high performer who is not being developed is being managed. The distinction is invisible from the outside and completely visible from the inside. The person who is delivering excellent work in a role that no longer stretches them has a specific internal score that their leader almost never asks about and that almost always predicts their departure.

Toni is a senior analyst. She is the best person on Rachel's team. Every deliverable is excellent, every deadline is met, every client interaction is positive. She has been in the same role for twenty-two months. Rachel has been meaning to have a career conversation with Toni for four of them.

◆

pages.title: MOVEMENT ONE THE CONVERSATION RACHEL HAS BEEN AVOIDING
pages.html:
MOVEMENT ONE THE CONVERSATION RACHEL HAS BEEN AVOIDING

Rachel: "I want to do something different today. I want to talk about your career specifically — not the current work, the work you want to be doing in two years."

Toni: "Okay."

The monosyllable is not enthusiasm. It is caution. Toni has had career conversations before. Most of them were framed as development and functioned as retention management.

Rachel: "I'm going to ask you a question and I want you to be honest rather than tell me what you think I want to hear. In two years — where do you want to be? Not what's available here. What would you choose if you could choose anything?"

Toni is quiet for a moment. She is deciding whether to answer the question or answer a version of it.

Toni: "Leadership. I want to manage people. I've wanted it for about eighteen months. I've been waiting for an indication that it was something this organization would support before I said it."

Rachel: "Why haven't you said it?"

Toni: "I've raised my hand for two projects in the last year that had leadership components. Both times I was told I'd be considered and both times someone else was put in the role. I drew a conclusion."

THE SCORE

The Real Answer — Toni's Actual Score Enters the Conversation

PROFIT 68 ▲ 6|LOVE 70 ▲ 6|TAX 44 ▲ 10

MOVE EVIDENCE MIRROR — MOVE 04

Rachel asked the right question and Toni answered it honestly — because Rachel's framing made honesty feel safer than the prior pattern had. "What would you choose if you could choose anything" is a different question from "what are your goals here" — the first opens genuine aspiration, the second invites the managed career narrative. Profit builds because the conversation has arrived at accurate information. But Tax builds significantly because Toni's disclosure includes an indictment: she raised her hand twice and drew a conclusion from the outcome. That conclusion — that leadership development was not available to her here — is the internal score that has been building toward departure. Rachel now has the information. The question is what she does with it.

pages.title: MOVEMENT TWO THE ACCOUNTABILITY
pages.html:
MOVEMENT TWO THE ACCOUNTABILITY

Rachel: "I owe you a direct response to that. The first project — Marcus was further along in his development arc for that specific role and it wasn't a judgment about your ceiling. I should have told you that clearly at the time and I didn't. The second project — honestly, it wasn't as deliberate a decision as you experienced it. We made a quick call in a planning meeting without fully thinking through who was developing toward what. That's a process failure and it cost you something. I'm sorry for both."

Toni does not respond immediately. She is deciding whether this is different from the prior pattern or continuous with it.

Toni: "What does 'I'm sorry' change?"

The direct question. The only question that matters.

Rachel: "On its own, nothing. So let me make it specific: I have a project beginning in Q1 that has a team lead component — three people, six weeks. It's not a promotion and it's not a guarantee. But it's real leadership experience and I'm offering it to you. Not considering you. Offering it. And I want to build a development plan around leadership specifically — what you need to develop, what opportunities we'll create, what the timeline looks like. That's the change."

THE SCORE

The Accountability — Apology Made Specific and Actionable

PROFIT 82 ▲ 14|LOVE 86 ▲ 16|TAX 20 ▼ 24

MOVE HONEST STRIKE + PATH FORWARD — MOVES 02 & 09

"On its own, nothing" is one of the most honest sentences in this book — it acknowledges that acknowledgment without action is insufficient and then moves directly to action. The Q1 project offer is the Path Forward: specific, near-term, with explicit framing that manages the expectation it creates. Love builds 16 points because Toni just saw a leader receive her disclosure — including the implicit indictment — and respond by expanding accountability rather than defending the prior decisions. The Tax drops because the conclusion Toni had drawn has been given a specific, concrete reason to be revised.

pages.title: MOVEMENT THREE THE HONEST EXCHANGE
pages.html:
MOVEMENT THREE THE HONEST EXCHANGE

Toni: "If the Q1 project goes well — what's the realistic path to an actual leadership role here?"

Rachel: "Eighteen months, if we develop deliberately. There's a senior analyst role that I think will convert to a team lead structure when we restructure next year. That is speculative — I can't guarantee that structure change. What I can guarantee is that I will actively advocate for you for leadership opportunities and that I will tell you honestly if I see something that would make that path harder. Including things you might not want to hear."

Toni: "I can work with that."

Rachel: "Good. And Toni — I should have had this conversation four months ago. That's on me."

Toni nods. The recruiter's call is now something she will not return. Not because the offer is definitive — it is not. Because Rachel ran the conversation that made staying worth trying.

THE SCORE

The Honest Exchange — The Path Exists and Both People Can See It

PROFIT 88 ▲ 6|LOVE 92 ▲ 6|TAX 12 ▼ 8

MOVE INTELLIGENCE TRANSFER + OWNERSHIP MOVE — MOVES 03 & 05

Rachel ran Move 03 in its career development form: she transferred specific intelligence about the realistic path, including the speculative element she could not guarantee and the honest developmental feedback she would provide even if unwelcome. Then she ran Move 05 one final time — "I should have had this conversation four months ago, that's on me" — not as a hedge but as a closure. Love is at its highest point because Toni has seen Rachel receive an implicit indictment, take accountability for it, convert the accountability into specific action, and commit to the kind of honest partnership that makes genuine development possible.

◆

The Termination

The conversation no leader is trained for and every leader eventually faces

The termination is the highest-Tax single conversation in leadership. It is also the one where the leader's internal score — their clarity about why this is necessary, their genuine care for the person's dignity, their preparation for the conversation — is most visible and most consequential.

Elena is letting Marcus go. The performance has not been there for ten months. The conversations have happened. The development plan was built and the gaps were not closed. This is not a surprise to Marcus. It should not be. Elena has prepared. She has cleared her internal score.

◆

pages.title: MOVEMENT ONE THE CLEAR OPENING
pages.html:
MOVEMENT ONE THE CLEAR OPENING

Elena: "Marcus — I'm going to be direct with you today because you deserve that. We are ending your employment, effective today. I want to walk you through the details and I want to give you the space to respond."

Marcus is still. He was not surprised. He has been not-surprised for three months.

Marcus: "Okay."

Elena: "Over the past ten months we've had four documented conversations about the performance gaps — specifically the analysis depth and the stakeholder communication. We built a development plan in July. The gaps haven't closed to the level the role requires. That's the reason. Not your character, not your potential in a different context — this specific role and this specific gap."

A pause. Elena does not fill it.

Marcus: "I knew it was coming. I've known for a few months."

Elena: "I know. I think on some level we've both been in that position. I'm sorry it got to this point. I want to tell you what support we're providing and answer any questions you have."

THE SCORE

The Clear Opening — Dignity in the Hardest Conversation

PROFIT 72 —|LOVE 70 —|TAX 30 —

MOVE HONEST STRIKE — MOVE 02 AT ITS MOST CONSEQUENTIAL

The termination conversation's score is different from every other conversation in this book because the goal is not to build the relationship — the relationship is ending. The score is measured in whether the person being let go leaves with their dignity intact, with clarity about what happened and why, and with the best possible setup for what comes next. Elena ran Move 02 correctly: she was direct in the first sentence, she named the specific reason without editorializing it into a character judgment, and she acknowledged that both of them had known this was coming. The score does not move dramatically in this opening because the conversation is not building toward a future together. It is closing one. The measure of quality here is precision and humanity, not score accumulation.

pages.title: MOVEMENT TWO THE FULL SUPPORT
pages.html:
MOVEMENT TWO THE FULL SUPPORT

Elena: "Here is what the company is providing: twelve weeks of severance, benefits through the end of that period, and an outplacement service. I will also provide a personal reference — not just an employment verification. I will tell anyone who calls what you're genuinely good at and where I see you succeeding."

Marcus looks at her. The reference offer was not what he expected.

Marcus: "What will you say?"

Elena: "That you are a strong relationship builder and that your work is thoughtful and detailed in the right context. That this role required a specific kind of fast-cycle analysis that was not the match. I'll say both things because both are true."

A longer pause.

Marcus: "I appreciate that you said both things."

Elena: "You deserve an honest reference, not just a kind one. Those aren't always the same thing."

THE SCORE

The Full Support — Honest Reference as the Final Love Act

PROFIT 76 ▲ 4|LOVE 84 ▲ 14|TAX 20 ▼ 10

MOVE HONEST STRIKE + INTELLIGENCE TRANSFER — MOVES 02 & 03

Elena ran Move 03 — Intelligence Transfer — in its most human form: she gave Marcus something he did not know to ask for. The honest reference that names both the strength and the mismatch is more valuable than the kind reference that says nothing specific. "You deserve an honest reference, not just a kind one" is the sentence that will stay with Marcus. It tells him that the person who ended his employment saw him clearly and respected him enough to communicate both. Love builds 14 points not despite the termination but because of how it is being conducted.

pages.title: MOVEMENT THREE THE CLOSE
pages.html:
MOVEMENT THREE THE CLOSE

Marcus: "Can I ask you something?"

Elena: "Yes."

Marcus: "Was there a point where this could have gone differently? Where I could have changed the outcome?"

Elena is quiet for a moment. This is the question that deserves a real answer.

Elena: "Yes. In the July development plan, if the analysis component had moved — even partially — I think we could have built a case for continuing. It didn't move enough, and I want to be honest with you that I don't fully know why. Whether it was the role, the development support, something about how the feedback landed — I'm not certain. What I'm certain of is that it didn't move and that the gap became unsustainable for the team."

Marcus: "I appreciate you answering that honestly."

Elena: "You asked an honest question. You deserved an honest answer."

The conversation continues for another fifteen minutes — logistics, transition, paperwork. When Marcus leaves the room, he carries something most people who are let go do not carry: a clear picture of what happened, a genuine sense that the person who made the decision saw him fully, and a reference that will serve him. The termination was not good. It was conducted well. Those are not the same thing.

THE SCORE

The Close — The Question That Deserved a Real Answer

PROFIT 80 ▲ 4|LOVE 88 ▲ 4|TAX 14 ▼ 6

MOVE HONEST STRIKE — MOVE 02

"I don't fully know why" is one of the most honest sentences a leader can say in a termination conversation, and most leaders never say it because admitting uncertainty in a decision they are accountable for feels like undermining the decision. It does not undermine it. It humanizes it. The score at the close of a termination is measured by whether the person leaving has what they need to move forward clearly. Marcus has it.

◆

The Executive Conversation

Before the problem becomes something you're managing instead of surfacing

The leader who only brings their executive good news has built a relationship on a foundation that cracks the first time the news is not good. The leader who builds the habit of proactive disclosure — of surfacing problems before they surface elsewhere — has the only executive relationship worth having.

Devon manages a product team. There is a quality issue developing on a client-facing product that Devon has known about for five days. His executive, Sandra, does not know yet. The issue is not yet public. Devon is calling.

◆

pages.title: MOVEMENT ONE THE PROACTIVE CALL
pages.html:
MOVEMENT ONE THE PROACTIVE CALL

Devon: "Sandra — I'm calling because there's something developing on the Henderson product that I want you to know about before it surfaces in a client escalation."

Sandra: "Tell me."

Devon: "The reporting module has a calculation error that affects any account with multi-currency settings. I found it in QA five days ago. We've been working on the fix and I'm confident we can have a patch in production by Thursday. But there are fourteen client accounts affected and I need to decide whether to proactively notify them before they notice or wait until the fix is live."

Sandra: "Why are you bringing it to me now instead of Thursday when it's fixed?"

Devon: "Because the notification decision has reputational implications that I want your input on. And because you should know about it now rather than hear about it from a client."

THE SCORE

The Proactive Call — The Leader Who Does Not Wait

PROFIT 88 —|LOVE 84 —|TAX 14 —

MOVE HONEST STRIKE + INTELLIGENCE TRANSFER — MOVES 02 & 03

Devon ran both moves before Sandra had to ask anything. He called before the problem became an escalation. He named the specific issue, the affected accounts, the fix timeline, and the decision he needed input on. The score does not move dramatically in this opening because Devon and Sandra already have a high-Profit, high-Love executive relationship — built by this exact pattern of behavior over time. The reason this conversation is in this book: it is the conversation that most leaders do not make. They wait for the fix. Devon's call is the alternative. And the score it produces over time is the reason to make it.

pages.title: MOVEMENT TWO THE DECISION AND THE CLOSING
pages.html:
MOVEMENT TWO THE DECISION AND THE CLOSING

Sandra: "Notify proactively. Before Thursday, not after. If a client finds it before you tell them, the story becomes a company that knew and waited. If you tell them before they find it, the story becomes a company that caught it and communicated immediately. The second story is worth the discomfort of the call."

Devon: "That's where I was leaning. I wanted to make sure I wasn't missing a reason to wait."

Sandra: "You're not. Draft the notification. I want to see it before it goes. And Devon — the fact that you called before Thursday is the right call. Keep doing that."

The conversation takes nine minutes. Devon leaves with a decision and an explicit acknowledgment from his executive that the proactive disclosure was the right behavior. This is the executive relationship at its healthiest.

THE SCORE

The Decision — The Executive Relationship at Full Expression

PROFIT 92 ▲ 4|LOVE 90 ▲ 6|TAX 8 ▼ 6

MOVE PATH FORWARD — MOVE 09

"Keep doing that" is the most important sentence in the movement — Sandra has explicitly reinforced the proactive disclosure behavior, which means Devon now knows that this behavior produces positive outcomes with this executive. The score at the end of this conversation is high not because of what happened but because of the relationship norm it reflects and reinforces: problems surface upward immediately, not when they are resolved. That norm, consistently maintained, is the foundation of the executive relationship that survives the problems that all organizations eventually face.

◆

The Peer Conversation

Where organizational politics live — or don't

Two leaders. A shared problem that both of them could own and neither of them wants to. The conversation that determines whether the organization works or whether it performs working.

Marcus leads product. Alicia leads engineering. The launch timeline has a conflict — product needs three more weeks of testing, engineering has committed to a date that is now in jeopardy. Neither of them made the commitment to the client. Both of them are accountable to it.

◆

pages.title: MOVEMENT ONE THE OPENING POSITIONS
pages.html:
MOVEMENT ONE THE OPENING POSITIONS

Marcus: "I need to tell you that three weeks of testing is not optional. We've had two significant post-launch defect incidents in the last eighteen months. I'm not moving the testing window."

Alicia: "I hear you. And the client commitment was made with the original timeline. If we go back now and extend by three weeks, that's a credibility conversation we have to have with a client who has already planned around our date."

Marcus: "That's a real concern. But the alternative is a defect incident in front of that same client three weeks after launch."

Both of them have made their positions. Both positions are legitimate. Both people know that the actual answer requires something different from defending a position.

Alicia: "We're going to keep talking past each other if we don't reframe this. What is the actual decision we need to make together?"

THE SCORE

The Opening Positions — Both Right, Both Stuck

PROFIT 62 ▲ 4|LOVE 66 ▲ 2|TAX 40 ▲ 6

MOVE FRAME RESET — MOVE 01

Alicia ran Move 01 — Frame Reset — by naming what was happening in the conversation rather than continuing to operate inside it. "We're going to keep talking past each other" is the highest-Profit sentence available in a peer leadership disagreement where both parties have legitimate positions. It declines the debate and proposes a shared analysis. The question "what is the actual decision we need to make together" is correct because it replaces two competing decisions with one shared one. Profit builds because both people have stepped out of position defense and into problem definition.

pages.title: MOVEMENT TWO THE SHARED ANALYSIS
pages.html:
MOVEMENT TWO THE SHARED ANALYSIS

Marcus: "The decision is: what is the minimum testing scope that gives us adequate defect protection, and can we reach that scope in the original timeline with additional resources?"

Alicia: "That's the right question. Tell me what the minimum scope looks like."

They spend twenty minutes on the specifics. Marcus identifies the two testing categories that account for eighty percent of historical defect risk. Alicia identifies two engineers who can be pulled from lower-priority work for ten days.

Marcus: "If we prioritize those two categories and add your two engineers — I think we get to adequate coverage in the original window. Not full coverage. Adequate."

Alicia: "What's the residual risk?"

Marcus: "Category three defects are underweighted. Those have been low severity historically. I'm willing to accept that risk if you are."

Alicia: "I'm willing to accept it if we document it and brief leadership so it's not a surprise if something surfaces post-launch."

Marcus: "Agreed."

THE SCORE

The Shared Analysis — Two Leaders Working the Same Problem

PROFIT 86 ▲ 24|LOVE 86 ▲ 20|TAX 12 ▼ 28

MOVE INTELLIGENCE TRANSFER + PATH FORWARD — MOVES 03 & 09

Both leaders ran Move 03 simultaneously — sharing the specific intelligence only they had (Marcus: the testing categories and historical risk weighting; Alicia: the available engineering capacity) in service of the shared problem rather than the individual position. Profit builds 24 points — the largest movement in this conversation — because the exchange moved from positional debate to genuine joint analysis. Love builds because both people demonstrated that they were capable of subordinating their individual concerns to the shared outcome. Tax drops because the impasse has been resolved not through one side conceding but through both sides contributing intelligence the other did not have.

◆

The Exiting Employee

The most honest conversation you'll have with someone on your team

The exit conversation is the one most leaders conduct as a formality and should conduct as a genuine scored exchange. The person leaving has information the organization needs and has no incentive to manage anymore.

Tyler has given notice. He is leaving for a competitor. His manager, Jordan, has requested an honest exit conversation — not the HR form, a real one.

◆

pages.title: MOVEMENT ONE THE REAL QUESTION
pages.html:
MOVEMENT ONE THE REAL QUESTION

Jordan: "I want to ask you something different from the standard exit questions. Not why you're leaving — I know the answer to that. What would have needed to be true here for you to stay?"

Tyler looks at Jordan for a moment. He was prepared for the standard questions.

Tyler: "You really want to know?"

Jordan: "I really want to know. I'm not going to use it to change your mind. You've made your decision and it sounds like the right one for you. I'm asking because I want to lead this team better after you're gone."

Tyler nods. The framing — "I'm asking because I want to lead better" — is what makes the honest answer possible.

Tyler: "Two things. More visibility into the decisions that affect my work — not consultation on everything, but knowing the reasoning behind major direction changes before they get announced. There were three this year where I found out the same time as external stakeholders and it felt like I wasn't trusted with the thinking. And development investment that was real and not just the language of development. I've been in the same scope for two years."

THE SCORE

The Real Question — The Exit Intelligence

PROFIT 80 ▲ 6|LOVE 78 ▲ 8|TAX 16 ▼ 4

MOVE DIAGNOSTIC OPENING — MOVE 03

Jordan ran Move 03 in the form of a genuine question designed to produce intelligence he does not have access to through normal channels. The framing — "I want to lead this team better after you're gone" — signals that the question is not retention theater. Tyler gave two specific, actionable observations: decision communication timing and development investment authenticity. Both are things Jordan can actually change. Both are things that, if changed, will affect the scores of the team members who remain. The exit conversation, run as a genuine scored exchange rather than a procedural formality, produces the most specific and honest developmental feedback available to a leader.

pages.title: MOVEMENT TWO THE HONEST ACCOUNTABILITY
pages.html:
MOVEMENT TWO THE HONEST ACCOUNTABILITY

Jordan: "The decision visibility — that's something I've been trying to improve and clearly not improving fast enough. The three announcements you're referencing — two of those were situations where I got late information myself and passed it on the same day. One of those I had earlier and I chose to wait for the formal channel. That was the wrong call."

Tyler: "Which one was it?"

Jordan: "The Q3 restructure. I knew two weeks before the announcement."

Tyler is quiet.

Tyler: "That was the one that mattered most. That's the one where I started updating my resume."

Jordan: "I know. In retrospect, I was protecting the organization's communication process over the relationship. That's a calculation I'd make differently now."

THE SCORE

The Honest Accountability — The Leader Who Names Their Own Decision

PROFIT 84 ▲ 4|LOVE 88 ▲ 10|TAX 12 ▼ 4

MOVE OWNERSHIP MOVE — MOVE 05

Jordan ran Move 05 with precision: he identified the specific decision, named the calculation he made, and named the calculation he would make differently. "Protecting the organization's communication process over the relationship" is an honest characterization of a real leadership choice that had a real consequence — Tyler began looking elsewhere. The Ownership Move in an exit conversation does not recover the person who is leaving. It recovers the leader's understanding of what happened and their ability to lead differently for the people who remain. Love builds 10 points because Tyler is leaving the organization having been genuinely heard by the person he worked for.

pages.title: MOVEMENT THREE THE FORWARD LOOK
pages.html:
MOVEMENT THREE THE FORWARD LOOK

Jordan: "The development investment piece — what would that have looked like? Specifically."

Tyler: "A conversation about where I was going, not just how I was doing. Once a quarter. Thirty minutes about a two-year arc, not the current sprint. I've never had that conversation here."

Jordan: "I'm going to build that for the team that stays. I want you to know that. Not as a reason to reconsider — you should go. But because your feedback is going into something real."

Tyler: "That's a good change."

The conversation ends twenty minutes later. Tyler leaves knowing his observations were received, not just collected. Jordan leaves with two specific changes to make to a team of seven people who are still deciding, every day, whether they are in the right place. Tyler's honest answer just made that decision easier for them, though they will never know it.

THE SCORE

The Forward Look — The Exit That Improves What Remains

PROFIT 88 ▲ 4|LOVE 90 ▲ 2|TAX 10 ▼ 2

MOVE PATH FORWARD — MOVE 09

Jordan ran Move 09 in the form of a specific commitment to the team that remains — building the quarterly career conversation that Tyler never had. "Your feedback is going into something real" converts the exit conversation from a procedural formality into a development investment. The exiting employee who knows their honest observation produced a concrete change for their former colleagues leaves with a relationship to the organization that is different from one that produced only a polite farewell. The exit conversation is the highest-leverage feedback loop available to a leader. Run honestly, it develops the entire team through the departure of one member.

◆

pages.title: PART FIVE
pages.html:
PART FIVE

The Drills

Score the leadership line. Every exchange either builds the team or costs it.

Leadership drills require attention to the audience beyond the direct exchange. Every leadership line is heard by more than one person — the person being addressed and everyone else in the room who is drawing conclusions about what this leader does and values.

DRILL 01

"Great work on that presentation."

Score this recognition. What is the Profit position of the leader who runs it?

ANSWER P +2 · L +4 · T 0

Love +4, Profit +2. Generic recognition is better than no recognition. It is not good recognition. The specific problem: "great work on that presentation" does not tell the person what was great, which means they cannot replicate the specific behavior that earned the recognition. Praise that cannot be replicated does not develop people. Replace with the specific: "The way you anticipated the CFO's objection in slide eight and pre-answered it before she could raise it — that was the move that changed the room. That's a skill." Same warmth. Specific. The person who receives this knows exactly what to do again.

DRILL 02

"Does anyone have concerns before we move forward?"

Score this meeting question. When does it build Love and when does it drain it?

ANSWER P varies · L varies · T varies

This question scores entirely based on the environment in which it is asked. In a room where expressing concerns has historically produced positive outcomes — where the leader has visibly engaged with critical feedback and adjusted course — this question builds Love and Profit. In a room where expressing concerns has historically been met with defense, delay, or quiet consequence, this question produces silence that the leader reads as alignment. The same four words. Completely different scores depending on what has happened in the prior six months. The leader who wants this question to produce honest answers must first produce the environment that makes honest answers safe.

DRILL 03

"I hear you, but we need to move forward."

Score this response to a team member's concern in a meeting.

ANSWER P -6 · L -8 · T +12

Profit -6, Love -8, Tax +12. "I hear you, but" is one of the most reliable Love-destroyers in leadership communication because the "but" signals that the hearing did not actually change anything. The team member has disclosed a concern and watched it be set aside. Tax builds because the team member now carries the concern with no legitimate outlet for it, plus the additional cost of having expressed it publicly and watched it be resolved without engagement. Replace with genuine engagement: restate the concern specifically, name why it is being addressed or why it cannot be addressed, and give the person something real back.

DRILL 04

"I should have been clearer about that."

Score this self-correction by a leader in front of their team.

ANSWER P +4 · L +16 · T -8

Love +16. This is Move 05 — the Ownership Move — in its most accessible form, and it is the single highest-Love-building line a leader can run in a team setting. The team member who sees their leader take accountability for an unclear communication learns two things simultaneously: that this leader does not require their direct reports to absorb the cost of leadership failures, and that accountability in this team is something the leader models rather than only demands. The leader who runs this line when it is true — not performatively, but when they actually should have been clearer — builds more trust in a single sentence than a year of correctly-framed one-on-ones.

DRILL 05

"What do you think we should do?"

Score this question from a leader to a direct report facing a problem.

ANSWER P +10 · L +8 · T -8

Profit +10, Love +8. This is the most underused move in leadership communication and the highest-Profit development question available in a one-on-one. Most leaders answer their direct reports' problems. The leader who asks "what do you think we should do" is running Move 04 — Evidence Mirror — in its development form: they are asking the person to engage their own judgment before receiving the leader's. Profit builds because the direct report is being treated as a thinking partner rather than as a problem-presenter. The single most common reason high performers leave: they stopped being asked questions that required them to think.

DRILL 06

"That's not the direction we're going."

Score this response to a team member's alternative proposal.

ANSWER P -6 · L -8 · T +12

Profit -6, Love -8, Tax +12. This response shuts down an alternative proposal without engaging with its content. The team member does not know whether it was evaluated or dismissed. Love drops because the dismissal without engagement communicates that the proposal was not worth examining. Tax builds because the team member now has to decide whether to raise alternatives in future discussions — and the evidence from this exchange suggests that raising them costs something without producing anything. Replace with genuine engagement: name the specific reason the alternative does not fit, acknowledge what is valid in the proposal, and where possible invite the person to apply their thinking to the chosen direction.

DRILL 07

"I don't know the answer to that but I'll find out."

Score this response from a leader asked a question they cannot answer.

ANSWER P +6 · L +14 · T -8

Love +14. This is the Honest Strike in its most basic professional form and it builds Love significantly because it is rarer than it should be. Leaders who admit not knowing something in front of their teams are running a specific kind of courage that the team tracks carefully. The leader who says "I don't know" without anxiety about what it communicates about their competence signals that intellectual honesty is valued over the appearance of omniscience. The commitment — "I'll find out" — must be kept with a specific timeline. The open-ended "I'll find out" that never produces a finding is worse than the original admission.

DRILL 08

"The team is struggling right now. I want to be honest with you about that."

Score this candid opening from a leader to their executive.

ANSWER P +12 · L +14 · T -10

Profit +12, Love +14. This is the proactive honest disclosure that produces the executive relationship worth having. The leader who is willing to tell their executive that the team is struggling — before the struggling becomes a crisis, before the executive learns it from another channel — is building the only executive relationship that survives genuine difficulty. Profit builds because the executive now has accurate information and can calibrate their own decisions accordingly. Tax drops because the executive is not going to be surprised. Surprise is the highest Tax in executive relationships.

DRILL 09

"Let me think about that and get back to you."

Score this response to a direct report's request or proposal.

ANSWER P +2 · L 0 · T +10

Tax +10 if no follow-up arrives within 24 hours. The response itself is neutral — deliberation is often correct. The Tax accumulates entirely in the follow-through. The direct report who receives "let me think about that" and then receives no follow-up has learned that this phrase is a deferral, not a deliberation. Every subsequent "let me think about that" produces immediate Tax because the pattern has been established. The leader who commits to a deliberation timeline — "I want to think about that. I'll have something for you by Wednesday" — and keeps it runs this line at zero Tax. The timeline is everything.

DRILL 10

"This is hard to say, but I need to say it."

Score this opener before a difficult piece of feedback.

ANSWER P +6 · L +18 · T -8

Love +18. This is one of the most powerful feedback openings available to a leader because it names the cost of the communication before the communication happens. The direct report who hears "this is hard to say" understands immediately that what follows is not routine feedback — it is something the leader chose to say despite the difficulty of saying it. That choice is a Love act. It signals that the leader is not telling them this because it is easy or required, but because they believe the person deserves the honest information even when delivering it is uncomfortable. The feedback that follows must be specific and developmentally framed — the "hard to say" opener creates a responsibility to deliver something that lives up to the weight it implies.
